entries.snippet: तमिलनाडु में चल रहे राजनीतिक घटनाक्रमों के बीच, पीएमके (पट्टाली मक्कल काच्छी) ने राज्य में हो रहे उपचुनावों से दूरी बना ली है, जिससे AIADMK (अन्ना द्रविड़ मुनेत्र कड़गम) को बड़ा झटका लगा है। उपचुनाव अब पांच-कोणीय प्रतिस्पर्धा में बदल गए हैं। सूत्रों के अनुसार, पीएमके पार्टी के भीतर एक धड़ा टीवीके (थलपति विजय की पार्टी) के साथ गठबंधन की वकालत कर रहा है। यह संभावना जताई जा रही है कि पीएमके चुनाव परिणामों के बाद अपने निर्णय की औपचारिक घोषणा कर सकती है। इस घटनाक्रम से साफ है कि राज्य की राजनीति में महत्वपूर्ण बदलाव संभव हैं और नई राजनीतिक साझेदारियों की संभावनाएं बन रही हैं। AIADMK पीएमके के इस कदम से नाराज नजर आ रही है।

entries.title: 'थलपति विजय की टीवीके सरकार के अहंकार को हम चूर-चूर कर देंगे', तमिलनाडु सीएम पर क्यों भड़के DMK प्रमुख स्टालिन
entries.snippet: तमिलनाडु की राजनीति में माहौल गर्मा गया है जब डीएमके प्रमुख एम.के. स्टालिन ने थलपति विजय की पार्टी टीवीके सरकार पर गंभीर आरोप लगाए। स्टालिन ने सरकार पर अहंकार में कार्य करने और जनता की भावनाओं की अनदेखी करने का आरोप लगाया। उन्होंने कहा कि "टीवीके की सरकार के घमंड को हम चूर-चूर कर देंगे।" विवाद की मुख्य वजह चेन्नई के पट्टिनपक्कम क्षेत्र में नए सचिवालय की प्रस्तावित योजना है, जिसे लेकर राजनैतिक विरोध बढ़ता जा रहा है। स्टालिन ने यह भी स्पष्ट किया कि टीवीके की नीतियों और निर्णयों से जनता में असंतोष बढ़ रहा है और डीएमके इस मुद्दे को विधानसभा में मजबूती से उठाएगी। यह बयान आगामी चुनावों से पहले डीएमके और टीवीके के बीच राजनीतिक टकराव को और बढ़ा सकता है।

entries.title: 'Have several doubts about Vijay': Prakash Raj reacts Tamil Nadu CM's first 120 days in office
entries.snippet: Actor and politician Prakash Raj has expressed skepticism regarding Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Vijay's performance during the first 120 days of his administration. While Raj acknowledged that it is too early to reach a definitive conclusion about Vijay's governance, he admitted to harboring "several doubts" about his leadership and decision-making approach. Raj’s comments reflect a cautious yet critical perspective on the new government’s early initiatives and effectiveness. Additionally, when asked about a recent meeting between actors Vijay and Ajith, Prakash Raj chose not to speculate, emphasizing that such interactions should not be overanalyzed. His remarks contribute to the ongoing public and media discourse surrounding the Tamil Nadu CM’s leadership and the political implications of high-profile celebrity meetings.

Two Tamil Nadu bypolls, one political paradox: Why Left is taking on Vijay
entries.snippet: In a complex political move, the Communist Party of India (CPI) and the Communist Party of India (Marxist) [CPI(M)] have opted to contest independently in two upcoming Tamil Nadu by-elections—Madurantakam and Dharapuram—despite continuing to support Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay's TVK government from the outside. The CPI will field a candidate in Dharapuram, and the CPI(M) in Madurantakam, with candidate announcements scheduled for Tuesday. While the official rationale is that the Left is not aligned with any of the prevailing alliances—TVK-led, DMK-led, or AIADMK-BJP—the decision has sparked internal criticism, with some party members questioning why they should contest if they ultimately support the TVK government. This seemingly contradictory stance underscores the Left's awkward political positioning since the Assembly elections, where they chose to back Vijay to prevent Governor's rule and fend off indirect BJP influence. Although CPI(M) state secretary P. Shanmugam insists the move does not endanger the government and classifies bypolls as a non-general election, the Left now faces the challenge of campaigning against government candidates while still ensuring the government's stability.

entries.snippet: In a complex political move, the Communist Party of India (CPI) and the Communist Party of India (Marxist) [CPI(M)] have opted to contest independently in two upcoming Tamil Nadu by-elections—Madurantakam and Dharapuram—despite continuing to support Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay's TVK government from the outside. The CPI will field a candidate in Dharapuram, and the CPI(M) in Madurantakam, with candidate announcements scheduled for Tuesday. While the official rationale is that the Left is not aligned with any of the prevailing alliances—TVK-led, DMK-led, or AIADMK-BJP—the decision has sparked internal criticism, with some party members questioning why they should contest if they ultimately support the TVK government. This seemingly contradictory stance underscores the Left's awkward political positioning since the Assembly elections, where they chose to back Vijay to prevent Governor's rule and fend off indirect BJP influence. Although CPI(M) state secretary P. Shanmugam insists the move does not endanger the government and classifies bypolls as a non-general election, the Left now faces the challenge of campaigning against government candidates while still ensuring the government's stability.

entries.snippet: In a complex political move, the Communist Party of India (CPI) and the Communist Party of India (Marxist) [CPI(M)] have opted to contest independently in two upcoming Tamil Nadu by-elections—Madurantakam and Dharapuram—despite continuing to support Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay's TVK government from the outside. The CPI will field a candidate in Dharapuram, and the CPI(M) in Madurantakam, with candidate announcements scheduled for Tuesday. While the official rationale is that the Left is not aligned with any of the prevailing alliances—TVK-led, DMK-led, or AIADMK-BJP—the decision has sparked internal criticism, with some party members questioning why they should contest if they ultimately support the TVK government. This seemingly contradictory stance underscores the Left's awkward political positioning since the Assembly elections, where they chose to back Vijay to prevent Governor's rule and fend off indirect BJP influence. Although CPI(M) state secretary P. Shanmugam insists the move does not endanger the government and classifies bypolls as a non-general election, the Left now faces the challenge of campaigning against government candidates while still ensuring the government's stability.

Bengal hots up: Congress's Nandigram candidate held after getting Mamata backing
entries.snippet: In a dramatic escalation of political tensions in West Bengal’s Nandigram, former Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee withdrew her faction's candidate for the upcoming October 6 Assembly bypoll and extended support to the Congress nominee, Milan Pradhan. Shortly after her endorsement, Pradhan was arrested in connection with a 2007 murder case linked to the Nandigram land agitation. This arrest sparked accusations of political vendetta from both the Mamata-led faction and Congress, who blamed the BJP for manipulating legal processes to disrupt opposition campaigns. The Election Commission had recently frozen the original Trinamool Congress (TMC) name and symbol, assigning separate identities and symbols to the Mamata and Arup Roy factions. Mamata condemned the EC’s decision and approached the Supreme Court contesting the freeze. Meanwhile, BJP’s Nandigram candidate Hasirani Rath, mother of Suvendu Adhikari’s late aide, is expected to be a key contender. Mamata claimed that her faction’s candidate withdrew due to threats and reaffirmed her alliance with Congress as part of the INDIA bloc. She accused the BJP of authoritarian tactics, alleging that thousands of her workers have been arrested and political activities are being stifled across Bengal. Legal and electoral battles are expected to intensify ahead of the bypolls.

entries.snippet: Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay's party, Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK), is convening a meeting on September 9 to formalize its post-poll alliance, tentatively called the "INDIA alliance." While this alliance gains momentum, the Congress Party has firmly reiterated its support for Rahul Gandhi as its prime ministerial candidate for the 2029 Lok Sabha elections, countering speculation over Vijay’s potential national candidacy. Tamil Nadu Congress Committee President Manickam Tagore and AICC General Secretary K.C. Venugopal emphasized that Rahul Gandhi will lead the national opposition bloc and discouraged confusing narratives around alternative prime ministerial faces. The TVK-led coalition, which is only three months into governance, had its first coordination meeting in July. A formal name and common minimum programme are expected outcomes of the upcoming meeting. While some TVK ministers have endorsed Vijay as a future PM, Congress views these endorsements as fan-driven rather than politically strategic. The coalition includes Congress, MDMK, and Viduthalai Chiruthaigal Katchi, with CPI(M) and CPI supporting from outside. Tagore highlighted Congress’s instrumental support in forming the TVK government and maintained that inclusion in the INDIA alliance would depend on TVK having Members of Parliament.

entries.snippet: Tamil Nadu Chief Minister and TVK Chief C Joseph Vijay announced that the ruling alliance will be named the 'Secular Social Justice Victory Alliance'. The announcement followed a meeting held at the TVK headquarters in Panaiyur. A significant development was the decision to relocate the Government Secretariat to Pattinapakkam, as declared in a separate government order. Notably, leaders from the CPI(M) and CPI, though supportive of the government, did not attend the meeting. Key attendees included Tamil Nadu Congress Committee President B Manickam Tagore, Rajya Sabha MP Praveen Chakravarthy, Assembly floor leader Tharahai Cuthbert, and leaders from parties like MDMK, VCK, and IUML. This was the second major meeting since the post-election coalition formed the government and aimed to formalize the alliance structure.

How an ideological battle led to the AIADMK-BJP split

parts:
Yes. There is a real strategic pattern here, but I would frame it differently from “RSS/BJP likes Vijay”.

The deeper explanation is that **Tamil Nadu politics has several different axes**, and RSS, BJP, Congress, DMK, AIADMK, TVK and the Left do not sit on a single left–right line.

As of **24 September 2026**, the evidence is particularly interesting because TVK is actually governing with Congress and smaller parties, while the CPI and CPI(M) have chosen to remain outside the formal alliance and are now contesting the coming by-elections separately. citeturn824954search2turn476155search5

## 1. First: RSS and BJP are not necessarily looking for the same thing

This is probably the most important part of your observation.

The BJP's immediate objective is electoral: seats, vote share, organisational expansion, government participation.

The RSS has a much longer-term social and ideological objective. A recent report explicitly described the RSS view of Vijay as considerably more positive than the BJP's view, arguing that the Sangh's long-term objective in Tamil Nadu is to weaken the hold of Dravidian politics. citeturn931439view0

That produces an interesting divergence:

**BJP:**  
“Vijay has taken the anti-DMK political space that we wanted.”

**RSS:**  
“Vijay has weakened the old Dravidian political monopoly. That itself may be useful.”

Those are not contradictory.

The BJP can therefore be unhappy about losing votes to TVK while sections of the RSS can be pleased that **DMK's ideological dominance has been broken**. The Quint's reporting quoted an RSS functionary saying, in essence, that Vijay's emergence represents the end of the old era of anti-Sanatana politics, and described the RSS as hoping for a government less hostile to Hindu institutions and the Centre. Those are attributed views, not established facts about the whole organisation. citeturn931439view0

---

# 2. Why TVK can be interesting to RSS even though TVK is explicitly anti-BJP

This is the paradox.

TVK's own ideological declaration is explicitly built around:

- secularism
- social justice
- Periyar
- Ambedkar
- caste abolition
- proportional representation
- state autonomy

and it explicitly identifies the BJP as an **“ideological opponent”**. citeturn186656search0turn186656search2

So TVK is **not an RSS ideological ally**.

But there is another difference:

### DMK is an established ideological ecosystem.

The DMK has spent decades building:

- Dravidian identity
- rationalist/anti-Brahmin political traditions
- opposition to Hindutva
- Tamil-versus-Centre political narratives
- organisational relationships with Left and minority parties.

TVK is different.

It is a new party whose central political proposition is largely:

> **“The old two-party Dravidian system has failed; we are replacing it.”**

That distinction matters enormously to an organisation thinking in decades rather than elections.

The current RSS analysis reported by The Quint was essentially that Vijay has **no “Dravida” in the party's name**, has not constructed his politics around hostility to Hinduism, and has shown willingness to engage with religious/cultural institutions. citeturn931439view0

That does **not** make TVK pro-RSS.

It makes TVK potentially **less structurally hostile to RSS's worldview than an entrenched DMK political culture**.

That is a very different proposition.

---

# 3. Think of the Tamil Nadu political chessboard in four dimensions

This makes the apparent weirdness much easier to understand.

| Axis | DMK | AIADMK | TVK | Congress | Left | RSS/BJP |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dravidian identity | Very strong | Strong | Deliberately weaker/new | Weak | Variable | Opposed |
| Hindu cultural politics | Secular/rationalist | Pragmatic | Secular, but less traditionally anti-Hindu | Secular | Secular/atheist tradition | Hindu nationalist |
| Class/Marxism | Not Marxist | Not Marxist | Not Marxist | Not Marxist | Marxist | Explicitly anti-Marxist |
| Centre–State tension | Often strong | Moderate/pragmatic | State-autonomy rhetoric | More national | Federalist | Stronger Centre/national integration |
| Relationship with BJP | Opposed | Historically transactional | Explicit ideological opponent | Opposed nationally | Strongly opposed | — |

The crucial thing is:

**RSS doesn't necessarily ask “Who is right-wing?”**

It can ask:

> “Who is weakening an ideological structure that has historically obstructed us?”

That produces alliances that look bizarre if you use only the left/right spectrum.

---

# 4. Why AIADMK is a particularly natural vehicle for BJP

AIADMK is easier for the BJP to work with than DMK because it has historically been much more electorally pragmatic about national politics.

In 2026, AIADMK formally led the NDA arrangement, with BJP contesting 27 seats while AIADMK contested 169. citeturn532211search0

At the same time, EPS explicitly insisted that the alliance was **electoral rather than ideological**, showing that even AIADMK is not simply a BJP subsidiary. citeturn532211search3

This is actually useful to understanding the relationship.

AIADMK provides:

**Tamil Dravidian legitimacy + anti-DMK machinery + an established statewide organisation**

while BJP provides:

**national infrastructure + central leadership + Hindutva/nationalist mobilisation + resources**

There is tension, but there is also complementarity.

For RSS/BJP, AIADMK is therefore a **bridge into Tamil Nadu's existing political culture**, rather than asking Tamil voters to suddenly become BJP voters.

---

# 5. Why DMK is particularly difficult for RSS

This isn't simply because DMK is “Left”.

DMK is **not a Marxist party**.

The conflict is much more cultural and civilisational.

The RSS worldview is centred around a Hindu civilisational conception of India. The DMK political tradition developed around:

- Dravidian identity
- rationalism
- anti-caste politics
- opposition to Brahminical hierarchy
- linguistic nationalism
- strong Tamil identity
- historically sceptical attitudes towards Hindu religious authority.

So from an RSS perspective, **DMK represents an entire political-cultural ecosystem**, not merely another competing electoral party.

The organisation's own writings are very explicit about its opposition to communism as well, and RSS has described Marxism/communism as an ideological system fundamentally different from its own worldview. citeturn931439search0turn931439search1

This is why “anti-DMK” and “anti-Left” can simultaneously be important to the RSS even though DMK and Left are not identical.

---

# 6. And here is where your Congress idea becomes interesting

Your observation is more plausible at the **strategic level** than at the level of formal ideology.

Congress and RSS are obviously deeply opposed on major questions of:

- secularism
- Hindu nationalism
- minority politics
- nationalism
- the constitutional interpretation of religion and state.

So there is no obvious ideological RSS–Congress alliance.

But Congress is a **much broader ideological coalition** than the Left.

It contains:

- social democrats
- economic liberals
- centrists
- nationalists
- regional power brokers
- religious minorities
- business interests
- welfare-oriented politicians
- traditional Congress conservatives.

That makes Congress inherently more flexible than a Marxist party.

The RSS itself has demonstrated that it is willing to engage Congress figures. Its website prominently defended Pranab Mukherjee's appearance at the RSS headquarters in 2018 and described dialogue with Congress figures as legitimate and desirable. citeturn964087search0

And RSS-linked thinker S. Gurumurthy has spoken favourably about Congress having broken away from alliances with the DMK and previously argued that Congress should build an independent Tamil Nadu political base. citeturn931439view0

That does **not** mean RSS and Congress have become allies.

It demonstrates something subtler:

> **RSS can distinguish between Congress as an ideological opponent and Congress as a political force whose behaviour may sometimes weaken another ideological opponent.**

That distinction is central to Indian politics.

---

# 7. Why the Left is different

This is where your hypothesis becomes especially interesting.

RSS and the Left have a much more fundamental organisational and ideological conflict.

The RSS is:

**society-first, culturally nationalist, Hindu civilisational, anti-Marxist**

The Marxist Left is:

**class-first, materialist, internationalist in ideological origin, explicitly Marxist**

RSS's own material repeatedly attacks communism in precisely these terms. citeturn964087search0turn931439search1

And the conflict isn't merely about economics.

It concerns:

**What is society?  
What is the nation?  
What holds society together?  
What is the role of religion?  
What is the basis of social organisation?  
What should replace caste?  
Who should control institutions?**

Those are foundational questions.

So an RSS strategist can potentially say:

> “I disagree profoundly with Congress, but Congress is not trying to replace society with Marxist class politics.”

Whereas the Left is much closer to a direct ideological competitor.

That does not make RSS and Congress natural allies. It means the **distance between RSS and Congress can sometimes be politically smaller than the distance between RSS and a strongly Marxist movement on a particular issue**.

---

# 8. Tamil Nadu has produced exactly the situation you are noticing

Look at what happened after the 2026 election.

TVK won **108 of 234 seats**. DMK won 59 and AIADMK 47. citeturn532211search1

TVK then formed government with Congress and support from VCK, IUML and the Left.

But by September:

**Congress + VCK + MDMK + IUML** participated in the formal TVK alliance structure.

**CPI + CPI(M)** stayed outside it and continued providing only external, issue-based support. citeturn824954search2turn824954search3

And now the Left parties are contesting the Madurantakam and Dharapuram by-elections separately from the TVK-led bloc. citeturn476155search5

So the configuration is becoming:

**TVK ↔ Congress**  
**TVK ↔ VCK/other secular parties**  
**Left ↔ TVK government, but outside formal alliance**  
**AIADMK ↔ BJP**  
**DMK ↔ opposition to TVK**

That is already much more complicated than the old:

> DMK + Congress + Left  
> versus  
> AIADMK + BJP

binary.

---

# 9. There is another extremely important distinction: BJP wants votes; RSS wants societal realignment

This may explain your intuition better than anything else.

Suppose Vijay permanently destroys the old DMK–AIADMK duopoly.

There are then several possible long-term consequences.

One possibility is:

**TVK becomes a new secular-centrist Dravidian successor.**

Another is:

**TVK becomes a broad Tamil populist party with weaker ideological hostility towards Hindu institutions.**

Another is:

**AIADMK fragments and parts of its political/social base move towards TVK.**

Another is:

**BJP gradually expands inside this fragmented non-DMK ecosystem.**

For the **BJP**, the immediate problem is that TVK has stolen much of the political space BJP wanted.

For the **RSS**, however, the destruction of a 59-year-old political monopoly can itself be strategically valuable.

That is exactly the distinction some current reporting is identifying. citeturn931439view0

---

# 10. Why “Congress + RSS against Left” would not actually be as strange as it sounds

Not as a formal national alliance. There is no evidence currently showing such a project.

But as a **temporary convergence around particular political objectives**, Indian history contains plenty of examples of otherwise incompatible forces cooperating against a common opponent.

The interesting distinction is:

### Ideological alliance

“We believe broadly the same thing.”

versus

### Strategic convergence

“We disagree about the destination, but at this moment we prefer the other side not to dominate.”

RSS and Congress could theoretically have the second kind of relationship on some specific issue without resolving the first.

And this is exactly why Indian politics cannot be mapped simply as:

**Left ← Congress → BJP → Right**

The real structure is closer to a multidimensional graph.

---

# 11. The really deep layer: RSS may be less interested in “BJP rule” than in destroying competing ideological monopolies

This is the part I think gets missed.

The RSS existed long before the BJP became nationally dominant.

Its strategic project is fundamentally about **social organisation and cultural influence**, whereas BJP is the electoral-political instrument associated with that ecosystem.

Therefore:

**BJP losing an election ≠ RSS necessarily losing strategically.**

Conversely:

**BJP winning seats ≠ RSS necessarily achieving its long-term objective.**

From that perspective, three things can happen simultaneously:

> **TVK hurts BJP electorally.**

> **TVK weakens DMK/Dravidian monopoly.**

> **RSS becomes more comfortable with the post-DMK political environment.**

All three can be true.

That is why the reporting that the **BJP is more anxious about Vijay while sections of the RSS are more optimistic** is so significant. citeturn931439view0

---

# 12. But I would NOT conclude that RSS has decided “TVK + AIADMK + Congress against Left”

That goes beyond the evidence.

There are three reasons.

First, **TVK officially calls BJP an ideological opponent**. citeturn186656search0

Second, Congress and BJP remain major national adversaries; current reporting even shows Congress resisting TVK's internal push to project Vijay rather than Rahul Gandhi for 2029. citeturn824954search0

Third, the Left is still supporting Vijay's government from outside. Its present quarrel is over alliance structure and political independence, not a complete break with TVK. citeturn476155search5turn824954search3

So I'd describe the current situation more precisely as:

> **The collapse of the old Tamil Nadu political structure is creating temporary overlaps between actors whose long-term ideologies remain substantially different.**

And the RSS is unusually well positioned to exploit such a situation because its time horizon is **decades**, not one election.

### The simplest way to understand it

Think of the competing objectives:

**DMK:** preserve Dravidian ideological dominance.  
**AIADMK:** recover the Dravidian opposition space.  
**TVK:** replace the old Dravidian duopoly.  
**Congress:** regain independent political relevance through TVK.  
**Left:** preserve independent Marxist political space.  
**BJP:** expand electorally in Tamil Nadu.  
**RSS:** alter the deeper social/ideological environment in which all of them operate.

Once you separate those objectives, the apparent RSS interest in Vijay becomes much less mysterious.

And there is a particularly interesting paradox:

**RSS may find a successful non-DMK TVK more strategically useful in the long run than a weak BJP alone — while the BJP itself may regard that same TVK as its biggest immediate competitor.**

That is probably the key to the puzzle you are noticing. citeturn931439view0
